Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BEIJING, China (CNN) -- Consumers in Beijing's malls and shops are shunning the milk and poultry sections -- for good reasons. Poultry products, including eggs, may be contaminated with melamine through animal food. They are shocked and scared by the news headlines: some food produced in China is tainted with melamine. "Of course I'm worried," says a woman shopping in Nanxiaojie Market. Stop eating eggs? "That's not possible," she tells CNN. "If there's a problem with eggs, it should be solved fundamentally." Chinese premier Wen Jiabao says China will take steps to win back consumers. "We will use our actions and high quality of our food products to win the trust and confidence of Chinese people and people around the world," he told reporters at the end of a two-day summit of Asian and European leaders in Beijing last weekend.  Watch more about the tainted food scandal » . "Three minister-level officials have resigned and a government investigation is going on. Whoever is responsible must be brought to justice. We need to protect the Made in China brand," said Chinese analyst Victor Gao. But the problem could be more pervasive. The state-run Nanfang Daily published an investigative story saying that adding melamine into animal feed has become an "open secret." The report said adding melamine into feed started in the aquatic farming industry five years ago, as a way of faking higher protein levels.  Learn more about chemical melamine » . It then spread into other agro-industries such as poultry. Even more shocking is the allegation that the melamine added is from industrial waste material. CNN contacted the Ministry of Agriculture about the story, but got no immediate response. Two years ago, reports revealed pet food exported from China to the United States was spiked with melamine and had sickened and killed dogs. Several weeks ago, the food scandal spread to milk, biscuits and candies. Now, it is tainted eggs. So far, no illnesses or deaths have been linked to eggs. Tests in Hong Kong last week showed eggs exported by a Chinese company are contaminated with excessive levels of melamine. In recent days three other brands of eggs have also been found to contain the chemical. Small wonder egg sales at the Xinfadi, a wholesale market in Beijing, dropped by 10 percent this week, according to the state-run China Daily. Chinese officials say the source of the problem is melamine, an industrial chemical used to produce plastics and fertilizer. Melamine is high in nitrogen. Unscrupulous milk suppliers would water down milk and spike it with melamine -- but in amounts that allowed it to still pass quality tests. Agriculture experts speculate that eggs tainted with melamine may be the result of tainted feed given to hens. That begs the question: if melamine was in the animal feed, will it make into the meat, and into consumers' bodies? Ingesting melamine in large doses over an extended period of time could cause kidney stones and other illnesses, agriculture and health experts say. But taking in a small amount of melamine poses no such danger. "If it's taken over a long period of time, maybe, but if it's ingested only for short period of time it does not pose harm on animals," says He Jiguo, a professor of food science and nutrition at the China Agriculture University. He says the animals that end up being slaughtered do not live that long and do not actually ingest enough melamine for it to build up in their systems. The dogs and cats that were sickened in the United States were probably eating treats and meals tainted with melamine over a long period of time, he explains. Until the situation is resolved, worried grocery shoppers in Beijing say they'll just have to eat fewer eggs and more bean-products, like soybeans.

outputs.L1:
BEIJING, China (CNN) -- Consumers in Beijing’s malls and shops are steering clear of the milk and poultry sections—and for good reason. Poultry products, including eggs, may be contaminated with melamine through animal feed.

Shoppers have been shocked and frightened by headlines reporting that some food produced in China is tainted with melamine.

“Of course I’m worried,” says a woman shopping in Nanxiaojie Market. Stop eating eggs? “That’s not possible,” she tells CNN. “If there’s a problem with eggs, it should be solved fundamentally.”

Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao says China will take steps to regain consumer confidence.

“We will use our actions and the high quality of our food products to win the trust and confidence of Chinese people and people around the world,” he told reporters at the end of a two-day summit of Asian and European leaders in Beijing last weekend.

Three minister-level officials have resigned, and a government investigation is under way.

“Whoever is responsible must be brought to justice. We need to protect the Made in China brand,” said Chinese analyst Victor Gao.

But the problem may be more widespread. The state-run Nanfang Daily published an investigative report stating that adding melamine to animal feed has become an “open secret.” According to the report, the practice began in the aquatic farming industry five years ago as a way to falsify higher protein levels.

It then spread to other agro-industries, including poultry. Even more alarming is the allegation that the melamine being added comes from industrial waste material.

CNN contacted the Ministry of Agriculture about the report but received no immediate response.

Two years ago, reports revealed that pet food exported from China to the United States had been spiked with melamine and had sickened and killed dogs. Several weeks ago, the food scandal spread to milk, biscuits, and candies. Now, it has reached eggs.

So far, no illnesses or deaths have been linked to eggs. Tests in Hong Kong last week showed that eggs exported by a Chinese company were contaminated with excessive levels of melamine. In recent days, three other brands of eggs have also been found to contain the chemical.

It is little wonder, then, that egg sales at Xinfadi, a wholesale market in Beijing, dropped by 10 percent this week, according to the state-run China Daily.

Chinese officials say the source of the problem is melamine, an industrial chemical used to produce plastics and fertilizer. Melamine is high in nitrogen. Unscrupulous milk suppliers would dilute milk with water and spike it with melamine—but in amounts that allowed the milk to still pass quality tests.

Agriculture experts speculate that eggs tainted with melamine may be the result of contaminated feed given to hens. That raises the question: if melamine was present in animal feed, could it make its way into meat—and into consumers’ bodies?

Ingesting melamine in large doses over an extended period of time could cause kidney stones and other illnesses, agriculture and health experts say. But consuming a small amount of melamine poses no such danger.

“If it’s taken over a long period of time, maybe, but if it’s ingested only for a short period of time, it does not pose harm to animals,” says He Jiguo, a professor of food science and nutrition at China Agriculture University.

He says the animals that end up being slaughtered do not live long enough, nor do they ingest enough melamine, for it to build up in their systems. The dogs and cats sickened in the United States were probably eating treats and meals tainted with melamine over a long period of time, he explains.

Until the situation is resolved, worried grocery shoppers in Beijing say they will simply have to eat fewer eggs and more bean-based products, such as soybeans.
outputs.L2:
BEIJING, China (CNN) — Shoppers in Beijing are avoiding the dairy and poultry aisles in markets and stores, and they have reason to be cautious. Poultry items, eggs among them, could have been exposed to melamine through contaminated animal feed.

Many consumers say they are alarmed by reports that some Chinese-made food products contain melamine. “Of course I’m worried,” a woman shopping at Nanxiaojie Market told CNN. Asked whether she would stop eating eggs, she replied, “That’s not possible. If there’s a problem with eggs, it should be solved fundamentally.”

Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao said the government would act to restore public confidence. Speaking to reporters last weekend in Beijing after a two-day summit of Asian and European leaders, he said, “We will use our actions and high quality of our food products to win the trust and confidence of Chinese people and people around the world.”

Chinese analyst Victor Gao said three officials at the ministerial level had stepped down and that a government inquiry was under way. “Whoever is responsible must be brought to justice. We need to protect the Made in China brand,” he said.

However, the issue may extend far beyond a few isolated cases. The state-owned Nanfang Daily reported in an investigative article that mixing melamine into animal feed had become an “open secret.” According to the report, the practice began about five years earlier in fish farming, where it was used to falsely raise apparent protein readings. It later moved into other agricultural sectors, including poultry production.

The report also included an even more disturbing claim: that the melamine being added came from industrial waste. CNN asked China’s Ministry of Agriculture for comment on the report but did not receive an immediate response.

Two years earlier, reports found that pet food shipped from China to the United States had been adulterated with melamine, causing illness and death in dogs. In recent weeks, the contamination scandal expanded to include milk, biscuits and candy. Now eggs have been added to the list. So far, no illnesses or deaths have been connected to eggs.

Testing in Hong Kong last week found that eggs exported by a Chinese company contained melamine above permitted levels. In the days that followed, three additional egg brands were also found to contain the chemical.

It is therefore unsurprising that egg sales at Xinfadi, a wholesale market in Beijing, fell by 10 percent this week, according to the state-run China Daily.

Chinese authorities identify melamine as the source of the problem. The industrial chemical is used in making plastics and fertilizer and contains a high level of nitrogen. Dishonest milk suppliers had diluted milk with water and then added melamine so the product would still appear to meet protein-quality standards during testing.

Agricultural specialists believe melamine-tainted eggs may have resulted from hens being fed contaminated feed. That raises another concern: if melamine entered animal feed, could it also pass into meat and then into people who eat it?

Experts in agriculture and health say that consuming large quantities of melamine over a long time can lead to kidney stones and other health problems. Small amounts, however, are not considered to carry the same risk.

“If it’s taken over a long period of time, maybe, but if it’s ingested only for short period of time it does not pose harm on animals,” said He Jiguo, a professor of food science and nutrition at China Agriculture University.

He explained that animals raised for slaughter generally do not live long enough, or consume enough melamine, for the chemical to accumulate significantly in their bodies. By contrast, he said, the dogs and cats that became ill in the United States were likely eating melamine-contaminated food and treats for an extended period.

Until the problem is settled, anxious shoppers in Beijing say they plan to cut back on eggs and eat more bean-based foods, such as soybeans.

Chinese consumers are increasingly avoiding milk, eggs, and poultry as fears grow that melamine contamination has spread beyond dairy products and into the wider food chain.

The concern began with the discovery of melamine in milk and infant formula, a scandal that sickened thousands of children and badly damaged confidence in China’s food safety system. Melamine, an industrial chemical used in plastics and fertilizers, can make food products appear to contain more protein than they actually do when tested by standard methods. It is not meant for human or animal consumption and can cause kidney stones and other serious health problems.

Government investigations and Chinese media reports have since suggested that the problem may not be limited to milk. Authorities have examined whether melamine was added to animal feed, raising fears that contaminated feed may have reached chickens and other livestock. Those worries intensified after reports of melamine being found in eggs, leading some consumers to stop buying not only dairy products but also poultry and egg products.

The possibility that melamine was deliberately mixed into feed has alarmed the public. If feed producers used the chemical to falsify protein readings, it would indicate a wider and more systematic failure in food production oversight. Such revelations would also suggest that contamination could move through the food chain, from feed to animals and then to products sold in markets and supermarkets.

The scandal has already led to official investigations, factory inspections, arrests, and resignations of officials accused of failing to prevent or respond properly to the contamination. Regulators have promised tougher supervision and more testing, but many consumers remain skeptical. For parents especially, the discovery of melamine in infant formula created lasting fear and anger, and new reports involving eggs and feed have deepened suspicions that official assurances may not be enough.

The crisis also threatens China’s international reputation. The phrase “Made in China” has already been damaged by previous product safety controversies involving toys, pet food, seafood, and other exports. A widening food safety scandal could further harm confidence among foreign consumers, importers, and governments, leading to stricter inspections and possible trade restrictions.

At the heart of the issue is public trust. Many Chinese consumers now question whether food producers, local officials, and national regulators can guarantee the safety of everyday products. Even if authorities succeed in containing the contamination, restoring confidence may take far longer. The melamine scandal has become more than a food safety problem; it has become a test of China’s regulatory system and of the credibility of the country’s food industry at home and abroad.

counterfactuals.output:
**China’s Melamine Scandal Spreads Beyond Milk, Raising New Fears Over Eggs, Poultry and Animal Feed**

**BEIJING, October 2008** — China’s widening melamine contamination scandal, which began with tainted infant milk powder and sickened hundreds of thousands of children, has spread to eggs and raised fears that the industrial chemical may have entered the broader food chain through animal feed.

The new concerns emerged after regulators in Hong Kong detected melamine in eggs produced by a major supplier in mainland China. The findings prompted recalls, emergency testing and renewed anxiety among consumers already shaken by the discovery that dairy producers had adulterated milk with melamine to make it appear higher in protein.

The scandal has become one of China’s most serious food-safety crises in years, exposing weaknesses in regulation, local oversight and supply-chain monitoring. It has also dealt another blow to public confidence in Chinese food products at home and abroad.

## From Milk Powder to Eggs

The crisis first erupted publicly in September 2008, when authorities confirmed that infant formula made by the Sanlu Group and other dairy companies had been contaminated with melamine. The chemical, normally used in plastics, resins and fertilizers, can falsely inflate protein readings in food-quality tests because it is rich in nitrogen.

Chinese health officials later reported that hundreds of thousands of infants and young children had suffered urinary problems, including kidney stones, after consuming contaminated formula. Several deaths were reported. The scandal led to the arrest of dairy executives and milk suppliers, the resignation or dismissal of officials, and recalls of Chinese dairy products in multiple countries.

But in late October, the crisis expanded beyond dairy.

Hong Kong’s food-safety authorities said they found melamine in eggs from the Dalian Hanwei Enterprise Group, a large egg producer based in northeastern China. The detected level reportedly exceeded Hong Kong’s legal limit. The discovery triggered immediate recalls and a suspension of sales of the implicated eggs.

The result was a new and troubling question: if chickens were laying eggs containing melamine, had the chemical entered poultry feed?

## Beijing Consumers React With Alarm

In Beijing’s food markets and supermarkets, shoppers reacted with a mixture of caution, anger and fatigue. Many consumers had already stopped buying certain milk powders and dairy snacks. The news about eggs prompted some families to rethink even basic staples.

At market stalls, customers asked vendors where eggs came from and whether suppliers had safety certificates. Some shoppers said they would buy only locally sourced eggs or eggs from brands they trusted, while others avoided eggs altogether.

Vendors in several Beijing markets reported slower sales, especially for packaged eggs from larger producers. Some stallholders tried to reassure customers by displaying inspection documents or saying their eggs came from small farms not linked to the implicated company. But many consumers remained unconvinced.

“I don’t know what is safe anymore,” was a common sentiment among shoppers. Parents of young children were especially worried, having already followed the milk-powder crisis closely and taken children for medical checks.

The spread of the scandal to eggs deepened public suspicion because eggs are widely consumed across China and used in countless prepared foods, from noodles and cakes to school meals and restaurant dishes.

## Government Orders Expanded Testing

Chinese authorities responded by ordering broader inspections of eggs, poultry products and animal feed. Local regulators were instructed to test farms, feed producers and food processors for melamine contamination. The central government also moved to tighten scrutiny of the dairy industry and strengthen quality-control procedures.

Officials emphasized that the situation was being investigated and that contaminated products would be removed from shelves. In some regions, authorities conducted spot checks at wholesale markets and supermarkets. Producers were required to trace supply chains and identify whether feed ingredients had been adulterated.

Hong Kong, which maintains its own food-safety system, moved quickly to test eggs, meat and other imports from mainland China. The discovery there increased pressure on mainland regulators to explain how melamine could appear in non-dairy foods.

Several countries that had already restricted or tested Chinese dairy imports expanded their surveillance of Chinese food products. The scandal damaged the reputation of Chinese exports and revived memories of earlier food and product-safety controversies.

## Health Risks: Kidney Damage and Stones

Melamine is not approved for use in food. By itself, small exposures may not immediately cause illness in healthy adults, but the chemical becomes dangerous when consumed in significant amounts or over time, especially when combined with related compounds such as cyanuric acid.

The main health risk is kidney damage. Melamine can form crystals in the urinary tract, leading to kidney stones, urinary blockage and, in severe cases, kidney failure. Infants are particularly vulnerable because of their small body size, developing kidneys and reliance on milk powder as a primary food source.

In the milk scandal, babies who consumed contaminated formula developed symptoms including difficulty urinating, blood in the urine, vomiting, fever and signs of kidney stones. Hospitals across China screened children after the scandal became public.

For eggs and poultry, experts said the risk depended on the concentration of melamine, the amount consumed and the duration of exposure. Occasional consumption of low-level contaminated eggs was considered less dangerous than repeated consumption of heavily contaminated infant formula. Still, the presence of melamine in any food product was treated as unacceptable because it indicated deliberate adulteration or contaminated feed.

## Tainted Feed Suspected

Investigators focused increasingly on the possibility that melamine had been added to animal feed or feed ingredients. In livestock and poultry production, feed is often tested for protein content using nitrogen-based methods. Because melamine is high in nitrogen, unscrupulous suppliers may add it to low-quality feed ingredients to make them appear richer in protein.

If chickens consumed contaminated feed, melamine could pass into eggs and possibly into meat. Similar concerns applied to pigs, fish and other farm animals.

The possibility of contaminated feed suggested the scandal was not limited to a few dairy suppliers but reflected a broader incentive problem in food and agriculture: testing systems that measured nitrogen rather than true protein could be deceived by cheap chemicals.

Authorities investigated feed mills and ingredient suppliers, including producers of protein powders and additives used in animal feed. The egg contamination cases strengthened suspicions that melamine had been used beyond the dairy sector.

## Public Trust Under Strain

The scandal placed China’s food-safety system under intense public scrutiny. Many citizens questioned why contamination had not been detected earlier and why local officials had been slow to act. Reports that complaints about sick infants had circulated before the crisis became public fueled public anger.

The government promised harsh punishment for those responsible and reforms to prevent future incidents. Dairy companies faced criminal investigations, and senior officials in affected regions were removed from their posts. Regulators also announced new standards for melamine limits in food and strengthened inspection requirements.

Still, public confidence remained fragile. In Beijing and other cities, many families turned to imported milk powder despite its higher cost. Some consumers began scrutinizing labels more carefully, while others avoided processed foods containing milk, eggs or protein additives.

## Wider Implications

The spread of melamine concerns from milk to eggs and poultry demonstrated how contamination in one part of the food system can quickly raise doubts about many others. Modern food supply chains are interconnected: farms rely on feed producers, processors rely on farms, and markets depend on inspection systems capable of detecting fraud.

The crisis also highlighted the limits of routine protein testing methods. Because melamine can mimic protein in standard nitrogen tests, regulators and food companies faced pressure to adopt more sophisticated testing techniques and conduct more frequent audits of suppliers.

For consumers in Beijing and across China, the immediate question was simple but difficult: which foods could be trusted?

As authorities expanded testing and recalls, the discovery of melamine in eggs turned a dairy scandal into a broader food-chain crisis — one that raised concerns not only about milk powder, but also about eggs, poultry and the safety of animal feed itself.

counterfactuals.output:
BEIJING, China (CNN) -- Chinese authorities expanded inspections of poultry farms and animal feed suppliers after eggs in several parts of the country were found to contain melamine, the industrial chemical at the center of a deadly tainted-milk scandal that shook consumer confidence across China and abroad.

The latest food-safety alarm began when Hong Kong health officials said routine testing had detected excessive levels of melamine in eggs imported from mainland China. Additional samples were ordered, and retailers were told to remove suspect batches from shelves while officials traced the products back to their suppliers.

Melamine, used in plastics, adhesives and laminates, can make food products appear to have higher protein content when tested by some common methods. It can also cause kidney stones and kidney failure, particularly in infants and young children.

The discovery in eggs has raised concerns that melamine may have entered the food chain through contaminated animal feed. Chinese state media and local officials have said investigators are examining whether feed producers added melamine or melamine-tainted ingredients to boost apparent protein levels.

The egg findings come only weeks after China acknowledged that melamine-contaminated milk powder had sickened hundreds of thousands of children and killed several infants. That scandal led to arrests, factory closures and the removal of numerous dairy products from store shelves in China and overseas.

Melamine contamination also drew international attention in 2007, when pet food ingredients exported from China were linked to the deaths and illnesses of cats and dogs in North America. Investigators in that case found melamine in wheat gluten and other protein additives used in pet food.

Hong Kong, which maintains separate food-safety controls from mainland China, has intensified testing of eggs, dairy products, meat and processed foods since the milk scandal emerged. Officials there said they would continue screening food imports and publish test results as they become available.

In Beijing and other Chinese cities, shoppers said the egg scare had made them more cautious. Vendors in some markets reported a sharp drop in egg sales, with consumers switching brands, buying smaller quantities or avoiding eggs altogether.

“I used to buy eggs every few days,” said one Beijing resident at a neighborhood market. “Now I want to know where they came from and whether they have been tested.”

Food-safety experts said the episode underscores weaknesses in China’s fragmented agricultural supply chain, where small farms, feed mills, middlemen and processors can make contamination difficult to trace.

“The key question is not only which eggs tested positive, but how melamine got into the chickens’ feed in the first place,” said one food-safety specialist. “If the contamination is in feed ingredients, the problem could extend beyond a single farm or brand.”

Experts also warned that repeated scandals have damaged public trust. Even when risks are limited to specific batches, they said, consumers often react broadly because they lack confidence in labeling and enforcement.

Chinese officials have promised tougher inspections, harsher penalties for producers who adulterate food and closer monitoring of feed manufacturers. But analysts say restoring confidence will require consistent enforcement and greater transparency about test results, recalls and the source of contamination.

For many consumers, the egg scare has revived a question left unresolved by the milk scandal: whether authorities can detect dangerous additives before they reach the dinner table.

**Beijing shoppers wary after melamine found in eggs**

**BEIJING, China (CNN-style report)** — Shoppers in Beijing are expressing renewed concern about the safety of Chinese food products after authorities found the industrial chemical melamine in eggs, widening fears that contamination may extend beyond dairy products.

At markets and supermarkets across the capital, some customers said they were avoiding eggs or buying only trusted brands after reports that melamine had been detected in eggs produced in parts of China. The findings come after a major food safety scandal involving melamine-tainted infant formula, which sickened hundreds of thousands of children and severely damaged public confidence in domestic food products.

“I used to worry about milk powder,” one Beijing shopper said. “Now I wonder what else is unsafe.”

### How melamine can get into eggs

Melamine is a nitrogen-rich industrial compound used in products such as plastics, adhesives and laminates. It is not approved as a food ingredient.

Food safety experts say melamine can enter the food chain when it is illegally added to animal feed ingredients to make them appear higher in protein. Standard protein tests often measure nitrogen content, and because melamine contains a high level of nitrogen, it can falsely boost test results.

If chickens eat feed contaminated with melamine, small amounts of the chemical can pass into their eggs. Similar contamination could theoretically occur in meat if livestock or poultry consume tainted feed, though the amount transferred depends on exposure levels, duration and the animal’s metabolism.

Another possible source is contaminated feed additives or protein concentrates, such as adulterated wheat gluten, rice protein powder or other feed components. In past contamination cases, melamine and related compounds have been found in animal feed ingredients.

### Does melamine in eggs or meat pose a risk?

Health specialists say the risk to humans depends on the concentration of melamine and how much contaminated food a person consumes.

Melamine is best known for its ability to combine with related chemicals, such as cyanuric acid, to form crystals that can damage the kidneys. Infants and young children are considered especially vulnerable because of their smaller body size and developing kidneys. The greatest danger in China’s milk scandal came from repeated consumption of highly contaminated infant formula.

For eggs and meat, experts say occasional exposure to very low levels is less likely to cause harm, but repeated consumption of foods with higher contamination could pose a kidney risk, particularly for children, pregnant women, the elderly or people with existing kidney disease.

International food safety agencies have established tolerable daily intake limits for melamine, and many countries set maximum allowable levels in food. Products exceeding those limits are typically recalled or banned from sale.

### Trust remains shaken

Chinese authorities have promised inspections and tighter controls on animal feed and food production. But for many consumers, the discovery of melamine in eggs has reinforced fears that contamination problems are not isolated.

Food safety advocates say stronger testing of feed ingredients is essential because contamination can occur before food reaches farms, processing plants or store shelves.

“Testing the final product is important, but it is not enough,” one food safety analyst said. “If contaminated feed enters the system, it can affect eggs, meat and other animal products.”

For Beijing shoppers, the issue has become deeply personal. Many say they are reading labels more carefully, seeking imported products when they can afford them, or cutting back on foods they once considered routine.

“I don’t know what to believe anymore,” another shopper said. “Food should be the one thing we can trust.”

**China’s Melamine Scandal Widens From Milk to Eggs as Beijing Consumers Grow Wary**

*By Staff Reporter*

BEIJING — China’s tainted food scandal widened this week as concerns over melamine contamination spread beyond dairy products to eggs and animal feed, deepening public anxiety and putting fresh pressure on regulators already struggling to restore confidence after the country’s contaminated milk crisis.

The latest alarm was triggered by reports that eggs sold in Chinese markets had tested positive for melamine, the industrial chemical at the center of the infant formula scandal that sickened hundreds of thousands of children and damaged the credibility of some of China’s best-known food producers. While authorities have moved to reassure the public that investigations are under way, the discovery has broadened fears that the contamination problem may be rooted not only in milk collection and processing, but also in the country’s wider animal-feed supply chain.

A key focus of the expanding inquiry has been the possibility that melamine was added to animal feed to artificially boost apparent protein levels. The chemical, used in plastics and fertilizers, is rich in nitrogen and can make diluted or substandard products appear to contain more protein when tested by conventional methods. In humans and animals, however, melamine can combine with other compounds to form crystals that may cause kidney stones, kidney failure and other serious health problems.

The **Nanfang Daily**, a prominent newspaper based in Guangdong province, reported in an investigation that melamine had been found in feed ingredients and that some producers had used additives designed to inflate protein readings. The newspaper’s reporting helped intensify scrutiny of the feed industry, raising questions about whether contaminated feed may have passed melamine into eggs, poultry and other animal products.

The **Ministry of Agriculture** has responded by ordering inspections of feed producers and animal farms, and by calling for tighter checks on additives used in livestock and poultry production. Officials have said they are investigating how melamine entered the food chain and whether the contamination was isolated or part of a broader pattern of adulteration. The ministry has also emphasized that the use of melamine in feed is illegal and pledged punishments for companies or individuals found responsible.

Still, official assurances have done little to calm many consumers, particularly in Beijing, where the milk scandal remains fresh in public memory. At supermarkets and wet markets around the capital, shoppers have been questioning vendors about the origin of eggs and whether they have been tested. Some customers say they have stopped buying eggs altogether, while others have switched to more expensive brands or sought out products they believe come from smaller farms.

At **Xinfadi**, Beijing’s largest wholesale agricultural market and a major hub for the city’s food supply, egg traders have reported weaker sales as public concern spread. Vendors said buyers were asking more questions than usual and that demand had been affected by fears of contamination. Although eggs remain a staple of Chinese households, schools and restaurants, even rumors of food safety problems can quickly influence purchasing behavior in a city where many families are already on edge.

“I used to buy eggs every few days, but now I don’t know which ones are safe,” said one Beijing resident shopping at a neighborhood market. “After the milk powder problem, people don’t trust what companies say. We want to see real testing.”

The scandal began with infant milk formula tainted with melamine, which was added to milk to disguise dilution and raise apparent protein content. The crisis led to widespread recalls, arrests and the punishment of officials and executives. But the emergence of melamine in eggs suggests that the problem may not be limited to deliberate adulteration of milk products, and may involve upstream ingredients used in animal agriculture.

Food safety experts say the feed supply chain is difficult to police because it includes numerous small producers, middlemen and farms. Protein powders, feed concentrates and other additives can change hands multiple times before reaching livestock operations. Without frequent testing and strict oversight, adulterated materials can move through the system undetected.

“The risk is not simply one product or one company,” said a food safety analyst familiar with China’s regulatory system. “If melamine is being used in feed materials, then regulators need to examine the entire chain — from chemical suppliers to feed mills to farms and markets.”

The Ministry of Agriculture’s inspections are expected to focus on feed mills, poultry farms and suppliers of protein additives. Local authorities have also been instructed to increase sampling of eggs and other animal products. However, the scale of China’s food production network poses a major challenge. The country relies on a vast and fragmented farming sector, where enforcement can vary significantly by region.

The widening scandal has also renewed criticism of China’s food safety oversight structure. Before the milk crisis, warnings about tainted dairy products reportedly went unheeded or were suppressed at local levels. Public anger grew after it emerged that some companies delayed reporting problems, and that local officials had failed to act quickly enough to protect consumers.

Now, many residents say they fear that contamination could be present in other everyday foods. In Beijing, parents in particular have voiced concern about what to feed their children. Eggs, milk and meat are common sources of protein in family diets, and doubts about their safety have left consumers feeling they have few reliable choices.

“I can avoid some snacks or processed foods, but children need milk and eggs,” said another Beijing shopper. “If these are not safe, what can we eat?”

Retailers and wholesalers are trying to limit the damage by pointing to inspection certificates and origin labels, though some consumers remain skeptical. In the wake of repeated food safety incidents, paperwork alone is often not enough to restore confidence.

The melamine crisis has become one of the most serious tests of China’s consumer safety system in years. It has damaged domestic brands, shaken public trust and drawn international attention to the country’s export controls. Several countries have already restricted or tested Chinese dairy products following the milk scandal, and further revelations involving eggs or animal feed could increase pressure on Chinese authorities to demonstrate that contaminated products are being contained.

For now, officials are urging calm while investigations continue. But in Beijing’s markets, the effects are already visible: cautious shoppers, anxious parents and vendors facing questions they cannot always answer.

The discovery of melamine in products beyond milk has transformed what began as a dairy scandal into a broader food-chain crisis. Whether authorities can trace the contamination to its source — and convince the public that the food supply is safe — may determine how long consumer fear continues to shadow China’s markets.
